entries.title: HyperNetworks

en.summary: Uses one neural network to generate the weights of another.
en.construction: A trained network generates the parameters of another network.
en.training: The weight generator is trained jointly with the target network.
en.execution: The target network runs with the generated weights.

entries.title: Learning to Generate Task-Specific Adapters from Task Description

en.summary: Introduces Hypter, which generates adapters from natural-language task descriptions.
en.construction: A description encoder and hypernetwork generate adapters for a text-to-text model.
en.training: The generator learns from tasks with descriptions and labeled examples.
en.execution: BART performs the task with the generated adapters.

entries.title: HyperTuning: Toward Adapting Large Language Models without Back-propagation

en.summary: Produces task-specific parameters for a frozen language model from a few demonstrations.
en.construction: HyperT5 generates prefix or LoRA parameters from task demonstrations.
en.training: Hyperpretraining and multitask training prepare the generator; the paper also studies further task-specific tuning.
en.execution: A frozen T5 model runs with the generated parameters.

entries.title: HINT: Hypernetwork Instruction Tuning for Efficient Zero- & Few-Shot Generalisation

en.summary: Turns instructions and examples into reusable prefixes, adapters, and encoded instruction representations.
en.construction: An instruction-conditioned hypernetwork generates modules, and instruction fusion caches the instruction representation.
en.training: Instruction tuning trains the generator and model to generalize across tasks.
en.execution: An encoder-decoder model uses the generated modules and attends to cached instruction representations.

entries.title: Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability

en.summary: Compiles RASP programs into transformer weights with known computational structure.
en.construction: A symbolic compiler translates each RASP operation into network components and assembles their weights.
en.training: Compilation constructs the weights without model training. A separate experiment trains a projection to compress the compiled model.
en.execution: The compiled transformer executes the specified sequence computation.

entries.title: Text-to-LoRA: Instant Transformer Adaption

en.summary: Uses a hypernetwork to generate LoRA adapters from task descriptions.
en.construction: A hypernetwork maps the task description to LoRA matrices.
en.training: The paper trains generators by reconstructing adapters and through supervised task learning.
en.execution: A base transformer performs the task with the generated LoRA.

entries.title: Code2LoRA: Hypernetwork-Generated Adapters for Code Language Models under Software Evolution

en.summary: Trains a hypernetwork to generate repository-specific LoRA adapters from source code and update them as commits arrive.
en.construction: Static maps an encoded repository snapshot to LoRA weights. Evo updates a GRU state with each commit diff and generates the weights from that state.
en.training: The hypernetwork learns across repositories through the frozen code model’s assertion-completion loss. New repositories receive generated adapters without per-repository fine-tuning.
en.execution: The code model uses the generated adapter without adding repository context tokens to each request.

entries.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions

en.summary: Proposes fuzzy-function programming: compile a natural-language function specification into a neural program, then reuse it locally. Establishes a compiler–interpreter interface and releases FuzzyBench.
en.construction: A large trained compiler produces a neural program from the function specification. Its fast compiler generates LoRA weights in one forward pass.
en.training: PAW specifically trains a neural compiler to generate programs. New functions compile without per-function gradient descent.
en.execution: A frozen lightweight interpreter loads the program and runs new inputs locally.

links.label: FuzzyBench train, validation and test data

profile.title: A programming interface for fuzzy functions
profile.html: PAW makes a function specification into a saved, reusable neural program. The program combines a readable pseudo-program with learned adapter weights; a frozen interpreter executes it on new inputs. The paper demonstrates log monitoring, intent navigation, semantic reranking, tool routing and a word game.

profile.title: The compiler and the interpreter
profile.html: PAW specifically trains a neural compiler to generate LoRA adapters that edit the frozen interpreter’s weights. The Sparks experiments use a general-purpose LLM, not specifically trained for this purpose, to reason about and edit weights. Both produce computations represented in weights, through different construction methods.

profile.title: Compile and run a function
profile.html:
The local compiler exports a .paw file for the Python SDK. Compilation requires a BF16-capable NVIDIA GPU; the repository recommends 16 GB of GPU memory. The compiler and reference model run sequentially. The interpreter is downloaded once for local execution.

Standard targets Qwen3-0.6B; Compact targets a GPT-2 interpreter with extended positional embeddings. Each checkpoint contains the trained compiler and LoRA mapper, not the interpreter. Use the matching runtime linked below. Start with the builder guide, SDK reference or playground.

profile.title: Data and evaluation
profile.html: The verified evaluation repository contains test and test_clean splits with specification, input and output fields. The separate dataset release contains training, validation and test splits. Test new functions on held-out inputs, then test their composition with ordinary code; see the evaluation guide.

entries.title: Compile by Training: Turning Natural-Language Specifications into Local Neural Functions

en.summary: Compiles a function description into a reusable local program by generating training examples and optimizing an adapter.
en.construction: Teacher models generate examples from the specification. Gradient descent refines the adapter initialized by PAW’s fast compiler.
en.training: Training happens at function compilation; the saved program runs without the teachers.
en.execution: A frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter runs the saved function locally without further teacher calls.

entries.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights

en.summary: A general-purpose LLM reads numerical weights, constructs networks, and edits a language model. Tool access varies by experiment, from no tools to Python and limited model executions.
en.construction: The LLM reasons about the computation and writes the numerical parameters. Larger experiments use a Python environment and forward-pass feedback.
en.training: The general-purpose LLM is not specifically trained for this purpose. The reported construction and editing procedures prohibit gradient descent and training loops.
en.execution: The constructed or edited network runs on new inputs.

profile.title: Read, construct and edit
profile.html:
Published on November 2, 2026, Sparks presents three operations: infer behavior from weights, write a network for a task, and modify an existing network. It connects small-network examples with language-model analysis and repair.

Its general-purpose LLM is not specifically trained for this purpose. PAW specifically trains a compiler to generate programs; Tracr constructs weights through formal compilation. The shared subject is programming neural computation through weights.

profile.title: Read the experimental conditions separately
profile.html:
Game identification and small-network construction use no tools. Language identification permits Python but no model forward pass. Go construction and Qwen repair permit Python and bounded forward-pass feedback. Qwen repair targets repetition loops in a specified model and evaluation setting.

The released logs include prompts, model responses, sandbox code, evaluations and network artifacts. The edited checkpoint documents the weight changes. A community demo compares base and edited outputs.

profile.title: Responses and independent tests
profile.html:
Matthew Honnibal challenges combining different tool and feedback conditions into one capability claim. Sean Goedecke questions the superhuman-research interpretation. The authors’ November 12 response explains their broader framing and addresses experimental comparisons.

Simon Willison repeats game identification with a local model. Goworek and colleagues test changed games, code-policy controls and shuffled weights. Read the experiment analysis for the connections between these results.

entries.title: Weight-Space Programming from scratch on simple tasks

en.summary: An LLM coding agent writes transformer weights for tasks such as addition, sorting, and parity, then revises the programs using evaluation feedback.
en.construction: The agent edits the architecture and parameter-setting code, runs the resulting model, and simplifies successful programs.
en.training: The algorithmic-task procedure uses closed-form parameter assignment. The report identifies fitting and evaluation leakage in its language-task runs.
en.execution: The written transformer generates its answer token by token.

entries.title: Can an LLM Actually Reason and Program about Neural Network's Weights or is it just memorization on steroids? Exploring "Weight-Space Programming"

en.summary: Audits whether zero-shot neural-weight interpretation reflects computation tracing or local arithmetic and familiar-dataset priors.
en.construction: The language model describes network behavior; controlled label permutations and unfamiliar datasets test those interpretations.
en.training: The tested networks are trained beforehand. The weight-reading sessions perform no training or model execution.
en.execution: No replacement network is produced; the study evaluates the validity of the model’s explanations.

entries.title: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback

en.summary: Builds reusable update programs that turn experimental measurements into persistent corrections to scientific predictors.
en.construction: An LLM writes an editor that estimates parameter corrections, validates candidates on feedback folds, and saves accepted changes.
en.training: The editor fits corrections from measured feedback; its numerical fitting is distinct from the LLM session that writes the editor.
en.execution: The updated predictor makes subsequent predictions; the editor can process later experimental feedback.

entries.title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations

en.summary: Studies direct weight editing across 16 searches, seven benchmark families, and two model scales, measuring held-out gains and transfer between tasks.
en.construction: A reasoning agent inspects parameters, writes weight updates, and selects a checkpoint using development feedback.
en.training: The editing search uses no gradient-based optimization. Each search has a budget of 50 successful forward-tool requests.
en.execution: The selected checkpoint answers held-out questions without the editing agent.

entries.title: Weight-Space Programming of Policies and Their Verification via Model Checking

en.summary: Combines LLM-written neural policies with probabilistic model checking and feedback-driven repair.
en.construction: The LLM writes policy weights and revises them using optional action examples and model-checking feedback.
en.training: Weight writing and repair use no gradient descent. Storm computes satisfaction probabilities for the modeled environment.
en.execution: The neural policy selects actions; verification applies to the specified environment model and requirement.

entries.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models

en.summary: An LLM agent constructs interpretable transformers and brain-encoding features by writing their computations and weights in code.
en.construction: The agent revises explicit computations and weights, then audits their interpretability and tests reconstruction from short descriptions.
en.training: The agent-written model forbids backpropagation and pretrained weights. Brain-encoding evaluation separately fits a ridge-regression readout.
en.execution: The constructed model predicts task outputs or brain responses without the writing agent.

entries.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers

en.summary: Evaluates language-model agents on 42 tasks covering weight reading, repair, construction, impossible edits, and data-free compression.
en.construction: An agent inspects parameters and submits answers or edited networks inside an operating-system sandbox.
en.training: The benchmark restricts optimization and meters permitted forward-pass access; task results are scored under fixed budgets.
en.execution: The benchmark evaluates the submitted artifact on the task requirements.

entries.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets

en.summary: Tests whether an LLM can infer a predictor from structured examples and write every network parameter as a literal number.
en.construction: The model reasons from the supplied rows and emits a sealed vector of weights and biases before evaluation.
en.training: Construction permits no optimizer, code execution, or trial evaluation; held-out data evaluates the frozen network.
en.execution: The frozen network predicts unseen rows without the constructing LLM.

entries.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor

en.summary: Uses LLM-written neural-network weights to repair and construct a tractor steering controller, with simulation and real-tractor evaluation.
en.construction: The language model reasons about closed-loop dynamics and writes numerical controller parameters, using bounded simulation feedback.
en.training: The weight-writing sessions use no gradient descent; the study compares their controllers with gradient-based and classical baselines.
en.execution: The neural controller steers the tractor without the language model in the control loop.

entries.title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement

en.summary: Separates LLM program construction from score-guided refinement in diffusion concept editing.
en.construction: The LLM writes code proposing update directions and protective contexts; a shared numerical fitter selects update coefficients.
en.training: The pipeline includes numerical coefficient fitting and evaluation feedback. The paper tests generated programs against matched hand-written and search baselines.
en.execution: The edited diffusion model generates images without the program-writing LLM.

entries.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers

en.summary: Compares fixed transformers with architectures designed by LLM weight writers, including sparse tables and associative-memory models.
en.construction: The LLM either writes weights for a fixed architecture or designs a forward computation and its parameters.
en.training: The writing protocol excludes gradient training and fitting on data; a separate trained-model comparison is reported.
en.execution: The written model answers inputs without the writing LLM.

entries.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming

en.summary: A frozen language model writes reusable programs that construct weight updates for trained networks.
en.construction: The language model writes Python code that inspects the network and constructs weight changes, using evaluation feedback to select candidates.
en.training: The main protocol uses direct computation and forward-pass feedback without gradient-based training; finite-difference experiments are reported separately.
en.execution: The edited network runs without the language model. The retained code can construct new edits for compatible networks.

entries.title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading

en.summary: Separates the Sparks experiments by raw-weight access, Python tools and forward-pass feedback, and challenges presenting them as one capability.
en.construction: Compares the setup and outcome of each reported experiment.
en.training: Examines gradient-free protocols while distinguishing tool access and evaluation feedback.
en.execution: Use the experiment-by-experiment comparison when interpreting the original claims.

entries.title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights

en.summary: Questions the superhuman-research interpretation of Sparks, examining input-layer heatmaps and the relationship between Qwen repair and established steering methods.
en.construction: Uses input-layer weight heatmaps and a methodological comparison to explain the reported behaviors.
en.training: Discusses direct edits and their relationship to conventional training; it does not report a new trained model.
en.execution: Read alongside the original experiments and their authors’ response.

entries.title: Weight-Space Programming — From Neural Programs to Qwen Repair

en.summary: An illustrated walkthrough of network construction, raw-weight interpretation and Qwen repair, with labs based on released experiment artifacts.
en.construction: Connects mathematical explanations to the Sparks experiments, released logs and published critiques.
en.training: Explains the differences between direct parameter construction, training and feedback-assisted editing.
en.execution: Work through the browser-based examples and follow the linked source artifacts.

entries.title: Awesome Weight-Space Programming

en.summary: A bilingual collection covering direct weight programming and related research in generation, editing, merging and continual learning.
en.construction: Organizes primary sources by research questions and provides an evidence matrix and evaluation guide.
en.training: Distinguishes direct weight programming from trained generators and other related methods.
en.execution: Use the collection to find papers, implementations and experimental comparisons.

entries.title: Awesome Weight-Space Programming

en.summary: A reading collection connecting direct weight programming, community experiments, compilers, weight generation and model editing.
en.construction: Provides an introductory reading route and notes about the experimental conditions of linked work.
en.training: Covers both gradient-free construction and the trained mechanisms that form related research lines.
en.execution: Follow the reading paths, primary papers and linked code.

entries.title: wsp — weight space programming

en.summary: Community experiment harnesses, agent prompts and results for explaining, constructing and modifying neural-network weights.
en.construction: Agents work through CLI harnesses with token budgets, hidden tests and recorded checks.
en.training: Uses gradient-free weight-writing protocols inspired by Sparks; individual experiments specify their tool budgets.
en.execution: The repository provides Python 3.12 and PyTorch setup instructions for CPU, CUDA and Apple MPS.

entries.title: Learning to Control Fast-Weight Memories: An Alternative to Dynamic Recurrent Networks

en.summary: An early weight-generating system: one network learns to change another network’s weights, using those changes as temporary memory.
en.construction: A slow network produces context-dependent changes to the fast network’s connections.
en.training: Gradient-based learning trains the controller to store and retrieve information through fast-weight updates.
en.execution: The changing fast network processes temporal sequences and retains information in its connections.

entries.title: A Neural Compiler

en.summary: Translates Pascal programs into neural networks that implement their computations.
en.construction: The compiler converts source programs into cellular code, which builds the corresponding network by graph rewriting.
en.training: Program compilation constructs the network rather than learning it from input-output examples.
en.execution: The resulting network executes the compiled program, including variables, procedures and data structures.

entries.title: Thinking Like Transformers

en.summary: Introduces RASP, a language for expressing sequence computations in terms of transformer operations.
en.construction: RASP programs combine selection, aggregation and elementwise operations to describe algorithms such as sorting and histograms.
en.training: The paper trains transformers to reproduce the programs. Tracr later provides a compiler that constructs transformer weights directly.
en.execution: RASP executes the specified sequence transformation; the trained transformers are evaluated against that behavior.

entries.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

en.summary: Re-runs the Sparks game-identification prompts with a local Qwen3.8 27B model, publishing commands and model responses.
en.construction: The model receives numerical weights and architecture information, then identifies the game without executing the network.
en.training: The session uses the existing general-purpose model without task-specific training.
en.execution: Willison reports successful identification of Pac-Man, Pong and Breakout, and a failed Freeway example.

entries.title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers

en.summary: Replicates weight construction and reading, then tests changed games, ordinary-code policies and shuffled-weight controls.
en.construction: The LLM encodes game-playing algorithms into network weights; separate experiments test what information it extracts from trained networks.
en.training: Construction uses the frontier model’s existing capabilities. Controlled comparisons separate algorithm design from training and weight interpretation.
en.execution: The authors locate successful behavior in encoded algorithms and input-layer cues, and test where those strategies fail.

entries.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: Response to Comments
entries.venue: Update to Sparks of Weight-Space Programming

en.summary: The authors’ response distinguishes weight-space programming as a capability from any single experimental method.
en.construction: Explains why raw-weight reasoning, Python-assisted analysis and feedback-assisted editing belong to the same proposed research direction.
en.training: Clarifies tool use and gradient-free experiments while discussing the broader role of learning and optimization.
en.execution: Addresses MinAtar baselines and Qwen repair, and distinguishes the reported results from a comparison against human researchers.

entries.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

en.summary: Studies a language model writing edits to its own model weights through reasoning, Python code and forward-pass feedback, with evaluations of self-improvement and repair of corrupted copies.
en.construction: A fixed Qwen3.5 editor instance inspects weight tensors, graded practice answers and hidden states, then writes and tests candidate weight edits.
en.training: The editing session blocks gradients and optimizers. The editor uses its existing pretrained weights; candidate edits are evaluated through forward passes.
en.execution: The selected weight changes are loaded into the target model for subsequent inference.

profile.title: Editing and evaluation
profile.html: The study compares Qwen3.5 models from 2B to 27B parameters. In the repair experiment, the undamaged model edits a corrupted copy. The 27B sessions test edits on practice mathematics before evaluation on held-out problems; every session starts from the base weights.

profile.title: Connection to Program-as-Weights
profile.html: Both methods produce persistent changes through model weights. PAW specifically trains a neural compiler to generate LoRA adapters that edit a frozen interpreter’s weights from a natural-language function specification. Self-rewriting uses a general-purpose LLM, not specifically trained for this purpose, to write and test edits to its own model weights.

entries.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights

en.summary: Uses a multimodal LLM editor to diagnose repetitive thinking in vision-language models and write weight repairs, guided by failing images, hidden states and evaluation feedback.
en.construction: A failure census and visual inspection tools guide independent editing sessions. A held-out practice set selects edits that reduce unfinished answers and improve accuracy.
en.training: The editing harness blocks gradients, optimizers and iterative fitting to a loss. The editor reasons over pretrained weights and forward-pass results.
en.execution: Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B run with the selected weight edits. Deployment combines edits with budget forcing when held-out evaluation selects that combination.

profile.title: Vision-language model repair
profile.html: The editor inspects practice images, attention maps and the effect of replacing an image with a blank image. The paper evaluates repairs across visual mathematics, multimodal reasoning, hallucination, object probing and GUI grounding. Independent editors locate repetitive behavior in middle-layer attention outputs.

profile.title: Connection to Program-as-Weights
profile.html: Keel and PAW change model behavior through weights. PAW specifically trains a neural compiler to generate LoRA adapters that edit a frozen interpreter’s weights from a function specification. Keel uses a general-purpose multimodal LLM, not specifically trained for this purpose, to diagnose failures and write weight repairs through an interactive editing session.
